title: The bardo
hook: teachings on the in-between after death; a text read aloud to the dying

segments.voice: Yesterday: exile, and your line, carried into exile. Did you name something you'd carry anywhere, and thank whoever carried it to you? Day three hundred seventeen.

Hospice nurses will tell you: near the end, people often ask for something to be read or played. A favorite song. A psalm. A letter from a grandchild. Hearing, the nurses say, may be one of the last senses to fade. Tibetan Buddhists have a whole text for that moment, meant to be read aloud beside the dying, and then beside the body, for days afterward. It speaks directly to the person who has died, in a calm voice, telling them where they are. Today: the bardo.
screen: `A SONG, A PSALM, A LETTER.` → `HEARING, AMONG THE LAST TO FADE.` → `A TEXT READ ALOUD BESIDE THE DYING.`

segments.voice: Bardo is Tibetan for the in-between, a gap between one state and the next. Tibetan teachers describe several: the in-between of this life, of dreams, of meditation, of dying, and then, after death, the stages before a new birth. They teach that this last passage can last up to forty-nine days. First, they say, comes a moment of clear light, like a cloudless sky. If it isn't recognized, visions arise, peaceful and then fierce, and finally the mind is drawn toward a new life. The text that guides this is called, in Tibetan, Liberation Through Hearing in the In-Between. Tradition says Padmasambhava composed it and hid it, and it was revealed in the fourteenth century by a treasure-finder named Karma Lingpa. In the West it's known as The Tibetan Book of the Dead, a title given by its first English editor in 1927. A lama or friend reads it near the one who has died, and its message, over and over, is simple: don't be afraid; these appearances are your own mind; recognize them, and be free. Buddhist traditions differ here, and it's worth saying who says what. Many Theravada teachers hold that rebirth follows immediately, without an in-between. The Tibetan schools, and some other Mahayana traditions, teach the in-between in detail, and in East Asia families also mark forty-nine days after a death. And Tibetan teachers add one more thing: every moment is a kind of bardo. Between jobs, between homes, between one breath and the next, things loosen, and change becomes possible. In between.
screen: `BARDO — THE IN-BETWEEN.` · `CLEAR LIGHT, THEN VISIONS.` · `LIBERATION THROUGH HEARING.` · `EVERY MOMENT A KIND OF BARDO.` · then, large: `IN BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: This one asks for a gentle heart, so go easy. If you're willing, reflect for a moment: at the very end, what would you want read to you? A verse, a song, a few words from someone you love. Just let one thing come. You don't need to decide anything. Then let it go, and notice the small gap at the end of each out-breath, the tiny in-between before the next breath comes. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Bardo. The in-between: in Tibetan teaching, the passage between death and rebirth, and every gap where change becomes possible.
Your line: in between. Today, notice one in-between moment, a doorway, a pause in a conversation, the minute after waking, and let it be open. Day three hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: In Tibetan communities a lama or trained friend often reads the Bardo Thödol aloud beside the dying and, after death, beside the body, and families hold rituals during the forty-nine days that follow; many Theravada communities hold merit-making ceremonies for the dead instead.

original.note: Tibetan bar do: the in-between, the gap between one state and the next.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Tibetan word for the afterlife.
what it means: an in-between: after death, and also every gap in life where change can happen.

what a scholar hears: bar do is often glossed 'between two'; the Bardo Thödol is a 'treasure' (terma) text, and Evans-Wentz named it The Tibetan Book of the Dead in 1927 after the Egyptian Book of the Dead.

sources.ref: Bardo Thödol (Liberation Through Hearing in the In-Between), revealed by Karma Lingpa

notes: The Evans-Wentz / Kazi Dawa Samdup 1927 English version may be public domain in the US, but its exact wording isn't quoted here.

Theravada view of immediate rebirth: some Theravada teachers allow an intermediate period; framed as 'many Theravada teachers'. Confirm.
'Hearing may be one of the last senses to fade' is a common hospice observation; kept hedged with 'may'.
